claims.text: Metal rollers and guide plates in hot-dip aluminum plating degrade rapidly through direct contact with molten aluminum.
Applying an alumina-based ceramic coating will significantly reduce corrosion during long-term exposure to high-temperature liquid aluminum.
The proposed coating is based on alumina (Al2O3).
The typical operating temperature for hot-dip aluminum plating is 700–800 °C.
Deposition of the coating will produce a continuous, dense ceramic layer.
The alumina-based coating is chemically inert under the stated molten-aluminum exposure conditions.
The alumina-based coating is thermally stable at the stated operating temperature.
A continuous, dense alumina-based coating acts as a physical barrier between molten aluminum and the metal substrate.
Alumina has high chemical inertness and a high melting point.
Alumina's chemical inertness and high melting point prevent molten aluminum from wetting the underlying metal.
The alumina coating prevents molten aluminum from reacting with the underlying metal.
Suppressing wetting and reaction between molten aluminum and the substrate mitigates corrosion and erosion.
Coated components will have a measurably lower corrosion rate than otherwise identical uncoated components.
Coated components will have a significantly longer service life than otherwise identical uncoated components.
Performance outside the typical hot-dip aluminum plating temperature range is untested.
